STRENGTHS: (1) Real, well-articulated problem: Parkinson's symptoms fluctuate, clinic snapshots every 3-6 months are unrepresentative, and there is no home-monitoring equivalent to diabetes devices. (2) Founder-problem fit: the neuroscience lead originated the idea from direct clinical observation at a movement disorders clinic; the CS founder built a functioning prototype (capture, scoring, clinician dashboard); a business founder handles operations. (3) Early commercial validation: a neurology practice paid for a pilot, which is meaningful traction for a student team and produced feedback. (4) Sensible go-to-market: selling B2B to small/mid-sized practices with faster purchasing cycles, and a web app with no download suited to an older patient population. (5) Low deployment cost and a clear differentiation versus wearables (no hardware, uses an existing camera). (6) Self-awareness: founders openly name key gaps (validation, reimbursement, regulatory, clinical advisor), and the funding ask maps directly to the biggest risks (validation study, legal/privacy, pilot expansion). (7) Plausible expansion path to essential tremor and other movement disorders, and a possible pharma data revenue line.

WEAKNESSES: (1) No clinical validation: scores are unvalidated against standard scales (e.g., MDS-UPDRS), and video-based accuracy is likely below dedicated sensors. This is the core product risk, since clinicians will not trust or act on unvalidated scores, and it is unclear whether the product fits an FDA definition of a medical device/SaMD, which could require clearance and a heavy regulatory burden the team has not scoped. (2) Reimbursement is unconfirmed: the pricing rationale ($15-25/patient/month) leans on RPM billing codes they have not verified; if clinics cannot recoup cost, willingness to pay and adoption are at risk. (3) Privacy/compliance exposure: storing patient hand videos is sensitive PHI (HIPAA, BAAs, consent, security), and the team has no compliance expertise; video storage costs are also significant and unmodeled, threatening margins at $15-25/month. (4) Weak market and financial rigor: no bottom-up sizing, vague statements like 'several thousand neurologists,' and a projection of ~$50K ARR at 10 clinics/200 patients (implies ~$21/patient/month) rests on untested assumptions; that scale is small and the path to a large business is unclear. (5) Adoption/engagement risk: relies on daily patient or caregiver compliance among older users with possible cognitive and motor impairment; retention and data quality (lighting, camera angle, medication timing) are unaddressed. Clinicians also face workflow burden and alert fatigue from added dashboards. (6) Team gaps: no physician, no regulatory or healthcare-business experience; the neurologist advisor is informal only. Founders are students with uncertain full-time commitment beyond graduation. (7) Company hygiene: legal entity not fully formed, founder equity split unresolved, no website, and very limited revenue funded personally. (8) Competition: validated FDA-cleared wearables exist, and larger digital health players could add video-based assessment; defensibility (IP, data moat) is not articulated beyond cost.

OVERALL: Strong problem, motivated founders, and early paid pilot make this an interesting idea-stage opportunity, but the unvalidated core technology, regulatory/reimbursement uncertainty, privacy risk, and team/entity gaps keep it high-risk. Investment interest is moderate: worthy of small, milestone-based support (validation study, legal setup, regulatory guidance) rather than a large commitment, with interest rising materially if validation shows strong correlation with clinical scales and reimbursement is confirmed.
